opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I've lived on both sides of it.

Robot learning, historically, came out of the robotics community. People there started from the robot itself: the arm, the gripper, the controller, the dynamics. Learning was brought in as a tool to solve specific problems that classical control and planning struggled with, like grasping unknown objects, contact-rich manipulation, or locomotion over rough terrain. The mindset was very much "I have this physical system, how do I make it work better with data?" Evaluation happened on real hardware, often with a handful of tasks, and the bar was whether the robot actually succeeded in the physical world.

Embodied AI, as it emerged in the vision community around 2017 to 2019, started from the opposite direction. We had just gone through the big success of deep learning on ImageNet, detection, segmentation, all passive perception from internet images. Many of us began to feel that this was not how intelligence really develops. A child doesn't learn by looking at labeled photos; it learns by moving, touching, and interacting. So the vision community asked: what if the agent has a body, can move through a space, and perception serves action? That's where you got navigation benchmarks, simulators like Habitat, AI2-THOR, iGibson, and later SAPIEN, which my group worked on for articulated objects. The emphasis was on scalable simulation, large benchmarks, generalization across many scenes and objects, and the connection between perception, semantics, and decision-making.

So the cultures differed. Robot learning valued real-world deployment and physical precision but was often limited in scale and diversity. Embodied AI valued scale, generalization, and standardized benchmarks but was often criticized, sometimes fairly, for staying in simulation and not touching the hard physics of real contact.

What's happened in the last few years is that these two are converging. Vision people realized that if you never close the sim-to-real gap, you're not really solving embodiment. Robotics people realized that without large-scale data and foundation-model-style generalization, you can't get beyond narrow demos. Today when we talk about embodied intelligence, especially with generalist robot models, vision-language-action models, and large synthetic data pipelines, it's really the fusion: the scale and generalization ambition from the vision side, combined with the physical grounding and hardware seriousness from robotics.

For me personally, coming from 3D vision, the key bridge was understanding the world in 3D: geometry, parts, articulation, affordances. That's what lets perception become actionable. And I think the most exciting questions now sit exactly at that intersection, how to get data at scale, through simulation and synthetic generation, that actually transfers to real robots doing real, dexterous work.

r001.rationale: The response describes Robot Learning as starting from the physical robot and using learning to solve robotics problems, but does not state that it can proceed without vision.

r002.rationale: It frames embodied AI as giving an agent a body to move through a space, with perception serving action, and identifies this as the vision community’s approach.

r003.rationale: The response says Robot Learning and embodied AI are converging and fusing, but does not clearly state that embodied AI later came to encompass Robot Learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Let me say first that these two terms, Robot Learning and embodied AI, really grew up in different communities, and that history shapes how people use them.

Robot Learning is the older term, and it comes from robotics. The robotics community has always had a clear object: a physical machine that has to perceive, plan, and act in the real world. For a long time the dominant approach was model-based control, where you write down the dynamics, do state estimation, and plan. Robot Learning emerged when people in that community started asking whether parts of this pipeline, or the whole pipeline, could be learned from data rather than hand-designed. So the identity of Robot Learning is defined by the robot. The question is always: how does this help a real system act better?

Embodied AI, as it emerged in the vision community around 2017 or 2018, came from a different direction. Vision researchers had done extremely well on static benchmarks like ImageNet and COCO, and there was a growing sense that perception alone was hitting a ceiling. Perception in biology was never passive. We see in order to act, and our actions change what we see. So the vision community wanted to close that loop. The natural way to do it, given their tools, was simulation. You got platforms like AI2-THOR, Habitat, Gibson, and tasks like embodied question answering, visual navigation, and rearrangement. The agent lived in a virtual environment and the body was often very abstract, sometimes just a camera that could move forward and turn.

So if I compress the distinction, I would say Robot Learning starts from the body and asks how to add intelligence, while embodied AI started from intelligence, or perception, and asked how to add a body. In the vision community's early version, that body was mostly a convenience for generating interactive data, not a physical system with contact, friction, and actuation noise.

That difference matters a great deal in practice. The robotics side cares intensely about things like sim-to-real gaps, control frequency, safety, and the fact that each real trial is expensive. The early embodied AI side could run millions of episodes and benchmark against each other on clean metrics. That gave it fast iteration, but it also meant a lot of results did not transfer, because the hard parts of physical interaction were never in the simulator.

What I find interesting is that the two are now converging. Once embodied AI researchers moved from navigation to manipulation, they ran directly into the problems roboticists had been dealing with for decades. Grasping a cup is not a camera motion. You need contact, you need dynamics, and you quickly need a real robot. At the same time, roboticists adopted the large-scale data mindset and the learning tools that vision and language people brought in. So today, when someone says embodied AI, they increasingly mean the whole thing: a learned policy, often a large model, running on a physical system.

My own view is that embodied AI is the more ambitious framing, because it is about the nature of intelligence, and Robot Learning is the more honest framing, because it never lets you forget there is a machine that has to work. I think the field is healthiest when it keeps both, the ambition of the first and the discipline of the second.

r001.rationale: The response describes Robot Learning as focused on helping a physical system act better, but does not say that it can operate without vision.

r002.rationale: It explains that perception is active, actions change what an agent sees, and the vision community sought to close that perception–action loop.

r003.rationale: It says embodied AI increasingly means the whole system, including a learned policy running on a physical platform, and describes the fields as converging.

astra-6.text:
I think the two overlap a lot, but they come from somewhat different starting points. Robot Learning starts with the robot: how can we use learning to give a physical machine the ability to perceive, make decisions, and act? The question is ultimately whether it can perform a task under real physical constraints.

Embodied AI, as it emerged in the vision community, starts more from a question about intelligence. Traditionally, vision systems receive an image or a video and produce a prediction. But an embodied agent can act, change its viewpoint, and change its environment. So perception becomes part of a loop: you perceive, you act, and your action determines what you perceive next.

That helps explain why a lot of early embodied AI work focused on navigation and interaction in simulated environments. You could study that perception–action loop without first solving all the hardware and control problems of a real robot. Robot Learning typically puts those physical problems much closer to the center.

I wouldn’t draw a hard boundary, though. Embodied AI doesn’t have to stay in simulation, and Robot Learning certainly uses simulation too. They’re increasingly converging around the same goal: agents that can learn to act effectively in the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception as part of Robot Learning but does not state that Robot Learning can work without vision.

r002.rationale: It frames embodied AI as a perception–action loop: agents act, change what they perceive next, and interact with their environment.

r003.rationale: The response says the fields are converging around a shared goal, but does not state that embodied AI later came to encompass Robot Learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they overlap a lot, but they come from somewhat different perspectives. Robot Learning starts with the robot: how can it learn to perceive, make decisions, and act? The emphasis is often on learning skills that actually work on a physical system, where you have to deal with contact, uncertainty, and hardware constraints.

Embodied AI, as it emerged in the vision community, starts more from the idea that intelligence shouldn’t just passively observe images. An agent should act in an environment, and its actions should affect what it sees next. That opened up questions around navigation, exploration, and interaction, often in simulation.

So I wouldn’t draw a hard boundary between them. An embodied AI agent doesn’t necessarily have to be a physical robot, and Robot Learning isn’t limited to visual perception. But when you ask an agent to manipulate objects and accomplish tasks in the real world, the two become very closely connected.

r001.rationale: It says Robot Learning “isn’t limited to visual perception,” explicitly communicating that it does not necessarily require vision.

r002.rationale: It frames embodied AI as an agent acting in an environment so its actions affect what it sees next, capturing the perception–action loop through which it emerged in the vision community.

r003.rationale: It says the fields become “very closely connected,” but does not state that embodied AI later came to encompass Robot Learning.
